posts.author: HoloM
posts.content_md:
Hello, 

i made a lasertransmission hologram today, (HeNe, with PFG-01, 20x30cm) The image is bright and incredibly deep ( you can see the wall at a distance of about 1,20 m) . It shows a figure which is made out of wood. But It has a small defect, and I can't explain why this is so. You can see a second ghost image of the figure, which is much less bright that the right one. It is located at the same height, but about 2cm to the left of the right picture. It's not cleary sharp, but you can see the contours. It looks like a shadow. Perhaps it's a kind of refelection. See the graphics:

Any hints or ideas???

posts.author: Kaveh
posts.content_md: My guess is your reference beam glanced off something, like a metal object, and you had a secondary but blurred reference beam. Look at the reference (or reconstruction) beam directly from where the film is and see if it is a pure spot or if there is a reflection from somewhere which is close to the direction of the ref beam.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
This often happens when a second source of light hits the film causing a second reference. If you're using a collimating mirror and a beam expander in front of a small mirror, so that you have small mirror -> beam expander -> collimator, then unless you iris off the light going into the expander, the collimator 'sees' the reflected light from the small mirror as well as the light from the expander. Both these point sources are collimated by the colliamtor and both provide a reference.

The fact that you can see the secondary image means that the secondary source is pretty bright. The fact that the second image is so close to the first means that the second reference is almost parallel to the intended reference and displaced by a small distance. The fact that the image size of the second, 'ghost' image is pretty much the same as the first, real image means that the second reference is travelling along the same path as the intended reference and has the same angle, it's as collimated or diverging as your intended reference. I'd say whatever mirror is the last mirror before the plate in the reference arm has a second reflection from somewhere.

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md: One diagnostiic to try is to use a lens to focus the reference beam onto a white card at at the plate location. It should form a single bright point, but if there are reflections you might see extra points. I mention this because I had been troubled by ghost fringes at the edges of my beam which turned out to be caused by internal reflections in the cylinder lens I use with my laser diode - I could see two spots on either side of the central focused spot. A couple of strips of black tape on the lens cured this.

posts.author: Kaveh
posts.content_md:
> **Martin:** What about a higher diffraction order?

Seems the image is very close to the primary image, and slightly blurred. A higher order would be just as sharp, and also would be at a much bigger angle away from that image.

posts.author: HoloM
posts.content_md: Ok, this sounds right, that there is a second reference beam. But from the collimating mirror I am sure that there is only one lightsource. It comes straight from the pinhole of my spatial filter. Do you think it's possible, that the reference Beam is reflected at the rear surface of the film holding glass plate? See attached picture.

posts.author: Kaveh
posts.content_md:
> **HoloM:** Ok, this sounds right, that there is a second reference beam. But fromthe collimating mirror I am sure that there is only one lightsource. It comesstraight from the pinhole of my spatial filter. Do you think it's possible, that the reference Beam is reflected at the rear surface of the film holding glass plate? See attached picture.

That would give you a reflection hologram. Also, the image would be sharp. The fact that your secondary image is blurred suggests a reflection from a slightly diffusing object, like a steel pole.

Did you put your head where the film is and look directly at the laser source (using a filter if it is too bright)? 

Here is another test. Look through the reconstructed hologram, back at the source. If there is still nothing around the reconstruction beam, then probably that is not the problem.

posts.author: HoloM
posts.content_md: Yes, you were right, thank you. I had a reflection of the beam after the spatial filter on the table surface. This then was formed by the collimating mirror to a second reference beam. The tip with the lens was very helpful.
